title: Fit drum brake shoes: short-lined primary forward, long-lined secondary rearward
instruction: These are the two rear drum brakes from one car, laid shoe side up on the bench with each anchor post on the far side. The white arrow on each backing plate points toward the front of the car from that brake. They are duo-servo brakes. Fit one primary and one secondary shoe to each backing plate, each shoe lying flat on a painted seat between the anchor post and the adjuster block, the way they go on this kind of brake, then let go of them.
context: Automotive service technicians (O*NET 49-3023) reline drum brakes routinely, and fitting the shoes the right way round is part of ASE A5 (Brakes) certification. On a duo-servo (Bendix-type) drum brake the primary shoe, with the shorter lining, goes toward the front of the car and the secondary, with the longer lining, toward the rear: in forward braking the primary is dragged round into the secondary, which does most of the braking. Shoes swapped front to rear change how the brake works and wear unevenly. Left and right brakes are mirror images, so with both plates the same way up 'toward the front' is on opposite sides of the two plates: a fitter who copies the first brake onto the second gets it backwards. Here both rear brakes of one car lie side by side on the bench (a half-size model), and the shoes have to be told apart by their linings and fitted the right way for each side of the car.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. A bench model, about half size (a 9 inch, 229 mm drum at full size), of the two rear duo-servo drum brakes of one car, laid shoe side up with the anchor posts on the far side. Everything except the four shoes is fixed to the table. (1) Two backing plates: dark grey steel discs 120 mm across and 6 mm thick, centred at x 35.0 cm, y +17.0 cm (the LEFT rear brake) and y -17.0 cm (the RIGHT rear brake). (2) On each plate an anchor post, a steel cylinder 10 mm across and 8 mm tall, centred 46 mm beyond the plate's centre (x 39.6 cm), and an adjuster block, a brass block 12 by 14 mm (x by y) and 8 mm tall, centred 46 mm in front of the plate's centre (x 30.4 cm). (3) On each plate two painted shoe seats, yellow paint 0.5 mm thick, each the filled footprint of a fitted shoe: one on each side of the line from the anchor post to the adjuster block (toward +y and toward -y), the shoe's centre line on a 46 mm radius round the plate's centre, its ends 10.8 mm clear of the post and 7.8 mm clear of the block. (4) Arrows, white paint 0.5 mm thick: one on each plate's centre (47 mm long, 16 mm wide at the head) and a larger one on the bench beyond each plate's far edge, centred at x 44.0 cm (100 mm long, 30 mm wide at the head), each pointing toward the front of the car: toward +y for the left plate and toward -y for the right plate (in a real set-up they are also marked FRONT). (5) Four loose brake shoes, 0.04 kg each, 3D-printed solid PETG painted light steel grey: curved bars 20 mm wide and 15 mm tall with flat tops and bottoms, inner radius 36 mm and outer radius 56 mm (centre line 46 mm), rounded ends, 140 degrees end to end along the centre line. Along the outer edge of each top runs the lining, a dark brown band 6 mm wide and 1 mm high (printed raised with the shoe and painted): over the middle 90 degrees of the arc on the two primary shoes (88 mm long at the outer edge) and over the middle 130 degrees on the two secondary shoes (127 mm). The shoes lie flat, lining up, in a row on the bench in front of the plates, convex side toward the plates (+x), the middle of each arc's outer edge at x 26.0 cm (each shoe spans x 21.9 to 26.0 cm and 98 mm in y), centred at y -33.0 cm (a secondary), -11.0 cm (a primary), +11.0 cm (a primary) and +33.0 cm (a secondary). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the four shoes' poses and both grippers (in a real trial: a steel rule, a protractor and a top photo once the arms have withdrawn). A shoe's mid-arc point is the middle of its centre line; its heading is the direction from its centre of curvature to that point, seen from above. Each seat's target: the mid-arc point 46 mm from the plate's centre straight toward +y or -y, the heading pointing the same way. 'Let go': at every step of the last 0.5 s no gripper's pad-tip point (midway between its finger tips) was lower than 10 mm above the shoe's top while within that gripper's finger reach of the shoe seen from above (65 mm fully open, 27 mm closed, over every yaw: a finger touching, pressing or propping it holds it). 'Settled': over the last 0.5 s the mid-arc point moved under 2 mm in all and the heading stayed within a 1 degree range. 'Still for 1 s': settled in each of the last two 0.5 s windows. A shoe is seated in a seat (fine) when it is let go and settled, lies flat lining up (tilted at most 5 degrees), its lowest point is within 3 mm of the plate's top, its mid-arc point is within 8 mm of the seat's and its heading within 8 degrees; seated (coarse): 14 mm and 15 degrees. A shoe turned concave side out is 180 degrees off and is not seated, nor is one upside down, on its edge, on a post or on another shoe. A seat holds a shoe when exactly one shoe is seated in it. A plate is correct when its seat on the arrow's side (toward the front of the car) holds a primary (shorter lining) and its other seat a secondary (longer lining), both seated at that level. First match wins: both plates correct (fine) and all four shoes still for 1 s: 1.0. Both plates correct (coarse): 0.75 (a shoe 8 to 14 mm or 8 to 15 degrees off, or the 1.0 layout not yet still for 1 s). Exactly one plate correct (coarse), the other unfinished, empty or with its shoes swapped: 0.5. Two or more shoes seated (coarse) anywhere but no plate correct: 0.25. Fewer than two shoes seated: 0. Examples: both brakes fitted primary forward: 1.0; the same with one shoe 11 mm off its seat: 0.75; the right brake fitted like the left (primary on its +y side, which is its rear), the mirror error: 0.5; one brake fitted, the other bare: 0.5; both brakes fitted primary rearward: 0.25; one shoe fitted: 0; the last shoe still gripped in its seat: that plate is not correct. Either primary may go on either plate, and either secondary. The trial ends early once 1.0 has held for 1 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, default friction. Return springs, hold-down pins, adjuster screw and parking-brake lever are left out, so each shoe lies on a painted seat between a fixed anchor post and adjuster block instead of being sprung against them, and each lining is painted on the shoe's top so its length shows from above. The model is about half size and its shoes are light plastic. Each shoe is one rigid body of a block and discs. The grippers are read only to check that each shoe was let go.
reset_notes: Lay the four shoes back flat, lining up, convex side toward the plates (+x), the middle of each arc's outer edge at x 26.0 cm: a secondary centred at y -33.0 cm, a primary at -11.0 cm, a primary at +11.0 cm and a secondary at +33.0 cm. The plates, anchor posts, adjuster blocks, painted seats and arrows are fixed. Nothing is consumed.
